extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing fantasy writers (urban fantasy and secondary-world fantasy)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for creating timeless urban fantasy and compelling secondary-world fantasy (including approaches with or without an explicit magic system). Focuses on what to include, what to avoid, and practical worldbuilding methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pinning urban fantasy to specific tech/pop-culture details
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not fix a contemporary urban-fantasy story to ephemeral technologies or pop-culture references that will date it (e.g., specific apps, memes, phone models, or fleeting music references). As the hosts put it: 'the phone is not the plot.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pull back a little — you can have characters using phones, but avoid naming apps, versions, memes, or other transient specifics. Anti-pattern: heavy reliance on contemporaneous cultural minutiae (e.g., dated song lyrics) which later readers will find opaque (example: Alan Dean Foster's Spellsinger books). Example of a tactic: Jim Butcher avoids tech details by making magic interfere with technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the hidden-world focus to reduce temporal specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Spend most of the story in the hidden/magical world rather than the contemporary one so modern technology and culture matter less (e.g., Harry Potter spends most time in the wizarding world).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the narrative primarily inhabits a secret or parallel world with its own rules and everyday life, contemporary temporal markers less often intrude. This is a safe way to keep a story feeling timeless even if set 'now.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly pinning time is an acceptable alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: You may choose to intentionally pin your story to a date or era (e.g., Seanan McGuire giving dates at chapter starts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaning in and committing to a time is a valid choice: be transparent about when the story is set rather than awkwardly trying to hide it. This approach accepts that the story is of its time but can still be enjoyed later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on timeless human concerns (character and stakes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the core of the story about things that are always important (character, relationships, emotions, fundamental conflicts), because those are what make a story 'timeless' regardless of peripheral details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If character arcs and universal themes are strong, readers will remain engaged even if superficial cultural details age. Examples cited: Dickens' and Bradbury's works remain readable despite dated specifics because of enduring emotional cores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer ubiquitous, enduring references over niche/pop-culture specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use references that are likely to be widely understood across time (e.g., Star Wars, Burger King) rather than fleeting local or niche cultural markers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ubiquitous references help ground readers without dating the story. Avoid hyper-local or ephemeral cultural markers that require contemporaneous knowledge to understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make place a character (invest in geography, culture, history)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat locations—the city, university, landscape—as active, character-like presences with distinct culture, history, and sensory detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build geography around conflict, show how history shaped institutions, and give the setting behaviors and quirks (examples: Rothfuss's University; evocative geography like the North Sea or Grand Canyon creating wonder). This helps the world feel alive and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide your position on the magic-system spectrum (explicit system vs numinous wonder)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consciously choose whether magic in your world functions like a systematic, science-like mechanism (permutation/exploration joys) or as numinous, implicit wonder (mystery, awe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each end of the spectrum appeals differently: a rigid system invites clever problem-solving (Brandon Sanderson-style), while numinous magic fosters awe (Lord of the Rings). Be aware readers will often try to infer patterns even if you don't provide a system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a secondary world compelling without a magic system by emphasizing history, politics, relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: You can create an exciting secondary world through political intrigue, cultural details, historical patterns, and interpersonal dynamics rather than relying on a defined magic system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Amberlough, Swordspoint, Guy Gavriel Kay. Use social structures, conflicts, and cultural texture to provide fascination and stakes in place of magical mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit scope of revealed worldbuilding; focus on what you love
rubrics_metrics.description: You don't have to explain everything—pick a handful of world elements that you are passionate about and make those rich and believable rather than exhaustively documenting every detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolkien built around language and myth because that was his passion; similarly, choose a few focal elements (language, food, trade, religion, geography) and develop them deeply. Avoid rabbit-holing into explaining every minor trait of the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the 'change one thing and follow permutations' worldbuilding method
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a single alternate historical or physical-change in the world and logically follow its cultural, economic, technological, and political permutations to generate believable differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example prompts: a meteor strike at a key moment; discovery of lead-to-gold alchemy. Go multiple levels deep—trace knock-on effects (economy, industry, classes, power shifts) to create organic and surprising world consequences. The hosts explicitly: 'Just change one thing, and then follow the permutations.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider and manage tech–magic interactions strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide how magic and technology interact in your setting and use that to your advantage (e.g., make magic interfere with technology to avoid dated tech details).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jim Butcher's tactic of having magic impair cell phones sidesteps the need to explain modern tech. Choose consistent rules for interaction so the world feels coherent and you can avoid unnecessary temporal detail where desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of market/audience implications of minimal or implicit magic
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary-world stories with little or no explicit magic may be more niche and possibly less broadly marketable than works with clear, explorable magic systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hosts note that books without overt magic (or with magic used sparingly) can still succeed but may appeal to a narrower audience; consider your audience and goals when minimizing magic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sensory and dramatic geography to create wonder without relying on magic
rubrics_metrics.description: Create scenes of physical wonder (storms, coasts, deserts, unique landscapes) and sensory detail (food, weather, architecture) to evoke awe and distinctiveness even when magic is minimal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describing being sandblasted on a North Sea shore or standing on the Grand Canyon can produce the sense of the 'strange' that draws readers in. Include sensory, visceral elements to sell the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show that the world is dynamic and has a past (history matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Convey that your world has history and change—institutions, past events, legends, economic shifts—so the setting feels lived-in and grounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use relics, social institutions, political tensions, and cultural memories to imply historical depth. This supports believable present conflicts and motivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't 'borrow trouble from the future'—avoid paralysis over being dated
rubrics_metrics.description: Worrying excessively about whether a story will be read in 20 years can prevent you from writing; focus on telling the story you want to write now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice: prioritize the narrative and characters rather than obsessing over future reception. Many successful works are rooted in their time yet remain compelling due to story and craft.
